input:
Before choosing a self-hosted deployment, decide who will be responsible for running it. Hosting the application yourself gives your team more control over its environment, but it also creates ongoing work. Someone needs to manage updates, investigate failures, maintain backups, and make sure the service remains available. These responsibilities should have clear owners before the application becomes part of everyday operations.

Start by identifying why your team wants to self-host. You might need to keep information within infrastructure you control, connect the application to internal systems, or meet specific operational requirements. Write those reasons down. They will help you decide which parts of the deployment matter most and whether the additional maintenance is justified.

Next, prepare a separate environment for testing. Avoid making your first deployment the one that everyone immediately depends on. A test environment gives you room to check configuration, understand the installation process, and observe how the application behaves. Record the steps you follow so another team member can repeat them without relying on your memory.

Access also needs attention. Decide who should be able to use the application and who should be able to change its configuration. Keep those permissions separate where possible. Store credentials through your approved process, and avoid placing them in shared documents or copying them into troubleshooting messages. When someone leaves the team, there should be a straightforward way to remove their access.

Plan recovery before you need it. Identify what must be backed up, how often backups should run, and where they will be stored. Then test whether you can restore the service using those backups. A successful backup job does not establish that recovery will work. The restore process needs its own check and documentation.

Updates should follow a similarly deliberate process. Review the relevant release information, test changes in the separate environment, and decide how you would return to the previous working version if necessary. Choose a maintenance window that limits disruption, and let affected users know what to expect.

Finally, document the basics in one place: ownership, deployment steps, access management, backup procedures, and the first actions to take when something fails. Keep this document practical enough to use during a stressful situation. Self-hosting works best when the team can explain how the service runs, recognize when it needs attention, and recover it without depending on one person who happens to remember everything from the original installation or the most recent update.
output:
Deciding to deploy a self-hosted solution requires determining who will be responsible for managing the deployment. While deploying an application yourself provides greater control over the environment in which it operates, it also results in continued responsibility. An individual (or individuals) will be required to perform updates, troubleshoot issues, create backups, and ensure that the service is always available. Prior to adding the application to your daily operation, assign these responsibilities to specific people.

Begin by listing the reasons your team wishes to deploy a self-hosted solution. Your organization may require keeping data within your own infrastructure; connecting the application to other internal systems; or meeting certain operational requirements. Once you have listed these reasons, you can determine which aspects of the deployment are critical and if the extra effort involved with maintaining the deployment is warranted.

Create a test environment. Deploying your application directly into production is never recommended. Creating a test environment allows you to verify configurations, learn about the installation process, and see how your application performs. Document each step taken during the deployment so that another member of your team can replicate the same steps without having to rely solely upon your recollection.

Consider access. Determine who has permission to utilize the application and who has authorization to modify the configuration. Wherever feasible, maintain separation between the two types of access. Use your organization's established method for storing credentials and do not place them in common files or include them in emails used for troubleshooting purposes. Develop a procedure to revoke access from former employees.

Develop a plan for recovering from disasters prior to experiencing a disaster. Establish what data needs to be backed up, how frequently backups should occur, and where backups should be kept. After establishing this plan, conduct tests to verify that you can successfully restore the service using your backups. Simply completing a backup job does not guarantee that you will be able to restore the service after a disaster. The restoration process also needs to be documented and tested.

Develop a similar formalized approach for performing updates. Review all pertinent release notes regarding new versions of your application. Install and test any modifications made to your application in a non-production environment. If necessary, identify how you would revert back to a previous working version. Schedule maintenance windows that minimize disruption to end-users. Notify those impacted by maintenance activities about expected downtime.

Lastly, compile all fundamental elements of deploying a self-hosted solution into a single document. Include information such as ownership, deployment procedures, access management policies, backup strategies, and initial responses to outages. Ensure that this document is easy-to-use under pressure. Deploying a self-hosted solution works best when the entire team understands how the service operates; identifies when it requires attention; and recovers it without relying on just one individual who remembers everything from the time he/she initially installed the application or last updated it.
